gaps: No fish or seafood of any kind — a large protein category completely absent.
No Korean, Japanese, or Chinese cuisine — East Asian cooking is nearly missing despite owning a wok and a Big Green Egg.
No egg-led mains — a fast, cheap vegetarian anchor that is missing.
Indian cooking appears only as a single South-Indian kanji; North Indian cuisine (the broader sub-cuisine) is untouched.
The Big Green Egg and Ooni are unused in the current list — no live-fire or slow-smoke projects.
Weeknight roster is thin on protein variety: only chicken appears once; pork and beef each once; no fish, no tofu, no eggs as a main.

ideas.title: Cantonese Steamed Fish
ideas.why: Fills the total absence of fish and introduces a classic Chinese steaming technique the carbon-steel wok was built for.

ideas.title: Easy Japchae (Korean Stir-Fried Glass Noodles)
ideas.why: Opens Korean cuisine entirely — a new country, a new noodle type (dangmyeon), and a new stir-fry technique; meat is simply omitted for the vegetarian.

ideas.title: Braised Eggs with Leek and Za'atar
ideas.why: Puts eggs at the centre of a proper main for the first time, deepens the thin Middle Eastern slot, and is on the table in under 30 minutes.

ideas.title: Dal Makhani (Restaurant-Style)
ideas.why: Fills the North Indian gap with a slow-cooked black lentil and kidney bean dish that rewards the Dutch oven or the Big Green Egg's low-and-slow capability.

ideas.title: Kare Raisu — Japanese Curry Rice with Chicken
ideas.why: Introduces Japanese cuisine and a completely different curry tradition (thick, sweet-savoury, roux-based) that nothing in the current list resembles.

ideas.title: Miso-Glazed Salmon
ideas.why: Adds salmon — a second fish protein and a new broiling technique — that is fast enough for weeknights and pairs naturally with the Japanese curry pantry already needed.
